front: ACL vs. firewall — which one limits what a specific system resource can access?
back: ACL. An ACL is a rule list that filters traffic by source/destination IP, port, and protocol, giving granular per-resource control. A firewall also filters on rules, but it guards a boundary rather than restricting an individual resource. When a question says limit what this specific resource can reach, answer ACL. When it says protect the network edge, answer firewall.

front: RPO vs. RTO — which is maximum acceptable DATA loss?
back: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) = how much data you can afford to lose, measured backward in time from the outage to your last good backup. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) = how long you can afford to be down. Memory hook: P for Point-in-time data, T for Time offline.

front: RTO vs. MTTR — both are about time. What is the difference?
back: RTO is a target you set: the maximum downtime the business will tolerate before consequences become unacceptable. MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) is a measurement of reality: the average time it actually takes to fix a failed device. RTO is a goal, MTTR is a statistic.

front: MTBF vs. MTTR
back: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) = average uptime between breakdowns — a reliability metric. MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) = average time to fix one once it breaks — a serviceability metric. Neither one has anything to do with data loss; that is RPO.

front: RFID vs. NFC vs. Bluetooth vs. Wi-Fi — sort by range.
back: NFC: 4 cm or less. RFID: up to about 30 cm (1 ft), tags carry ~2 KB, read-only-ish tracking. Bluetooth: 2–10 m, peer-to-peer file transfer. Wi-Fi: up to ~150 m, high throughput, the only one that can move large files. Pick by the distance and the payload size in the stem.

front: Evil twin vs. rogue access point
back: A rogue AP is any AP attached to the network without permission — an employee plugging in their own AP counts. An evil twin is a rogue AP that specifically mimics the legitimate SSID to lure clients and eavesdrop. If the stem says the AP is made to look like it belongs on the network, it is an evil twin.

front: ARP spoofing vs. MAC spoofing — both redirect Layer 2 traffic. How do you choose?
back: ARP spoofing poisons the ARP cache so one victim's gateway binding points to the attacker — targeted, affects only that host. MAC spoofing the gateway address would pull traffic from every host on the subnet. If the stem stresses that only one person is affected, answer ARP spoofing.

front: ARP spoofing vs. IP spoofing vs. evil twin — quick sort
back: ARP spoofing: Layer 2, on-path attack on a LAN. IP spoofing: Layer 3, forged source address to hide identity or impersonate. Evil twin: wireless only. The layer named in the question is usually the giveaway — 'Layer 2 traffic destined for the gateway' means ARP.

front: IP scanner vs. port scanner vs. protocol analyzer vs. NetFlow analyzer
back: IP scanner: which hosts exist — pings the address space and reports responders. Port scanner: which services are open on one host. Protocol analyzer: what is inside the traffic. NetFlow analyzer: traffic flow volumes and patterns. To find a rogue device, you want an IP scanner.

front: TAP vs. network sniffer
back: A TAP (Traffic Access Point) is inline hardware that copies traffic passively — it does not disturb the link, which is why it wins any question that says without disrupting operations. A sniffer captures packets too, but it sits on a host or SPAN port and can perturb the flow. Both capture; only the TAP is seamless.

front: Detect vs. prevent — a manager wants to know about unauthorized datacenter access.
back: If they want to detect, the answer is video surveillance. Badge readers, smart cards, and biometrics prevent access, but they cannot detect a person who used a stolen valid credential. Scan the stem for detect/identify/know-about versus stop/prevent/restrict before you look at the options.

front: Authoritative vs. non-authoritative DNS server
back: Authoritative: holds the original zone files and records for its domain — the source of truth. Non-authoritative: answers from cached results of queries it previously forwarded, so it does not hold the original data. A server that improves efficiency by caching is non-authoritative.

front: Recursive DNS server vs. recursive lookup vs. authoritative server
back: A recursive server does the legwork on the client's behalf, querying other servers until it reaches the authoritative source. That process is a recursive lookup. 'Authoritative lookup', 'primary lookup', and 'secondary lookup' are not real DNS terms — if you see them as options, they are filler.

front: Primary vs. secondary DNS server
back: Primary holds the original read-write zone records. Secondary holds a read-only copy and refreshes it via zone transfer from the primary. Secondaries are not for external queries only, are not caching-only, and do not split the namespace — they are backups.

front: Insufficient wireless coverage vs. signal degradation
back: Insufficient coverage: specific areas where signal is too weak or absent — a map problem. Signal degradation: quality falling off with distance or obstruction — a quality problem. If devices drop connection in certain parts of the office while the network is confirmed operational, it is coverage.

front: Anomaly alerting vs. IPS — which catches sophisticated threats that trip no alarm?
back: Anomaly alerting. It baselines normal behavior and flags deviation, so novel threats surface. An IPS blocks what matches a known signature, so anything new slips past. If the stem says might not trigger traditional security alarms, signature-based tools are wrong by construction.

front: Granular trap vs. verbose trap (SNMP)
back: A granular trap carries a single OID and its value — one key-pair about one event. A verbose trap carries all available data about the event, so it uses more bandwidth. 'A single key-pair value' in the stem means granular.

front: Administrative distance vs. metric
back: Administrative distance compares routes learned from different routing protocols — lowest AD wins, because AD ranks how much you trust the protocol. Metric compares routes within a single protocol. Multiple protocols offering the same destination is always an AD question.

front: BGP vs. VRRP for redundancy
back: BGP reroutes between autonomous systems, so it keeps sites reachable when a WAN link dies. VRRP is a first-hop protocol — it fails over the default gateway for internal clients only, and does nothing for WAN routing. WAN outage across sites means BGP.

front: BGP vs. OSPF
back: BGP is an exterior gateway protocol (EGP) that exchanges routes between autonomous systems — the internet's routing protocol. OSPF is an interior gateway protocol (IGP) using link-state and SPF inside one AS. Anything crossing organizational or ISP boundaries is BGP.

front: VLSM vs. FLSM vs. route aggregation
back: VLSM allows subnets of different sizes inside one network, matching each segment to its host count. FLSM forces uniform subnet sizes. Route aggregation is the separate act of consolidating subnets under a single advertised route. VLSM still requires subnet masks; it does not assign addresses — DHCP does.

front: Exploit vs. vulnerability vs. virus
back: Vulnerability: the weakness or flaw itself. Exploit: the technique or code crafted to take advantage of that weakness. Virus: a category of malware, which may or may not use an exploit. 'Crafted to exploit vulnerabilities' is the definition of an exploit.

front: WPA2-CCMP vs. WPA2-TKIP
back: CCMP (Counter Mode CBC-MAC Protocol, AES-based) replaced TKIP and is the real WPA2 security standard. TKIP carried WPA's weakness forward into WPA2-TKIP, so it is never the most secure option offered. Ranking worst to best: Open < WEP < WPA < WPA2-TKIP < WPA2-CCMP.

front: Voice VLAN vs. QoS vs. native VLAN for prioritizing VoIP on access ports
back: Voice VLAN is the direct, purpose-built answer when the question is about switch ports where VoIP phones connect. QoS does prioritize traffic but is the broader mechanism, not the port configuration being asked about. Setting a native VLAN for voice is not the practice.

front: Link aggregation vs. load balancing
back: Link aggregation bundles multiple physical links between two devices into one logical link for more bandwidth and redundancy. Load balancing distributes traffic across servers or paths. Aggregation does not encrypt and does not reduce broadcast domains — that is VLAN segmentation.

front: NAT Gateway vs. Internet Gateway in a VPC
back: NAT Gateway: lets private instances reach out to the internet without being reachable from it. Internet Gateway: connects the VPC to the internet in both directions, exposing resources. VPN Gateway: encrypted tunnel to your own network. Direct Connect: private dedicated circuit.

front: VPN vs. SD-WAN vs. CDN vs. VPC peering
back: VPN: extends network services across cloud and on-prem with an encrypted tunnel — the answer whenever security of data in transit is named. SD-WAN: optimizes enterprise WAN traffic. CDN: distributes content geographically. VPC peering: connects two VPCs to share resources.

front: 110 block vs. 66 block
back: 110 block: Cat 5 and above, wider terminal spacing to cut crosstalk — the answer for modern MDF/IDF data cabling. 66 block: older, analog voice. F-connector is coax; RJ-11 is telephone. For Cat 5e or better, always 110.

front: PDU vs. UPS vs. generator vs. HVAC
back: PDU: distributes power efficiently to racks — many outlets, amperage management. UPS: battery bridge for the seconds-to-minutes after mains failure. Generator: long-term replacement power. HVAC: temperature and humidity. 'Distribute power to racks' is a PDU, not a UPS.

front: Pre-action vs. wet pipe vs. clean agent fire suppression
back: Wet pipe: water always in the pipes, sprinkler alone releases it. Pre-action: requires both a detector actuation and a tripped sprinkler before water flows — that double condition is the tell. Clean agent (FM-200, inert gas): no water, minimal equipment damage, no environmental penalty — best for a datacenter.

front: Clean agent vs. halon
back: Both suppress without water. Halon is very effective but environmentally harmful and largely phased out. Clean agents like FM-200 achieve the same protection without the environmental concern, so any question mentioning environmental impact resolves to clean agent.

front: Single-mode vs. multimode fiber — and the naming trick
back: Memory aid: "S is not single." If the standard's name contains Base-S (10GBase-SR) it is multimode, short wavelength. Otherwise (10GBase-LR) it is single-mode, long reach. Base-T names are copper.

front: DHCP scope vs. reservation vs. lease time vs. option
back: Scope: the range of addresses handed out — create one per department to segment. Reservation: a fixed address tied to one MAC. Lease time: how long an assignment stays valid. Options: extra parameters like gateway and DNS. Segmenting ranges is always a scope question.

front: Split tunnel vs. full tunnel VPN — what actually differs?
back: Routing behavior, not encryption strength, protocol, or authentication. Split: only corporate-bound traffic goes through the tunnel; internet traffic goes direct, saving bandwidth. Full: everything is tunneled — more secure, more latency and load.

front: Lightweight vs. autonomous/standalone AP
back: Lightweight APs depend on a central wireless controller, which is what makes seamless roaming and centralized management possible across a large site. Autonomous and standalone APs each run their own config independently. Mesh APs interlink wirelessly but still lack central control.

front: Static vs. dynamic routing — which side owns which trait?
back: Static advantages: low router overhead, simple in small or high-security networks, predictable. Static disadvantages: poor scalability in large networks, and every topology change needs a manual update. Watch for questions that ask for the disadvantage and then list two advantages as bait.

front: Honeypot vs. CVE vs. botnet
back: Honeypot: a deliberately vulnerable host set up to attract attackers so you can study their techniques. CVE: a public reference database of known vulnerabilities — a website, not something you deploy. Botnet: a collection of compromised machines under an attacker's control.

front: SAML vs. TLS vs. IPsec vs. SOAP for SSO
back: SAML exchanges authentication and authorization data between trusted parties — the SSO standard. TLS secures the transport. IPsec secures IP communications. SOAP is a general structured-message protocol. Only SAML is about the auth data exchange itself.

front: Microwave vs. satellite vs. cellular vs. HF radio in mountainous terrain
back: Microwave wins on least latency with high throughput over the shorter hops between peaks. Satellite has inherent latency from the distance to orbit plus weather fade. Cellular coverage is unreliable in remote terrain. HF radio is slow and interference-prone.

front: Broadcast domain vs. collision domain on one unmanaged 24-port switch
back: 1 broadcast domain, 24 collision domains. Every switch port is its own collision domain. Only routers and VLANs split broadcast domains, and an unmanaged switch does neither. A managed Layer 3 switch could, which is why the word 'unmanaged' is load-bearing.

front: Change management documentation vs. release notes vs. network diagram
back: When something worked yesterday and fails today after a known change, read the change management documentation first — it records exactly what was altered and what it touched. Release notes describe the vendor's software generally; diagrams describe topology, not what changed.

front: Site survey vs. network diagram vs. topology — before estimating AP count
back: Site survey. It assesses the physical environment — walls, interference, coverage — which is what determines how many APs you need and where. Diagrams and topology documents are produced after the survey settles AP placement.

front: Patch management vs. HIDS vs. AUP vs. incident response team
back: Repeated infections through known vulnerabilities call for patch management — a technical control that closes the hole. A HIDS only detects effects. An AUP is an administrative control. An IR team responds after the fact. 'Prevent future outbreaks' plus 'known vulnerabilities' equals patching.

front: Data loss prevention policy vs. AUP vs. remote access vs. password policy
back: DLP policy governs how data may be shared and what gets inspected before it leaves — including automatic inspection of outbound email attachments. AUP governs user behavior, remote access governs connection methods, password policy governs credentials.
